# R6 — Late Travel Narrative §5.5–5.6 (Luke 13:10–19:27)

**Range read in full:** raw lines 8341–9440 (slice complete, 1100 lines)  
**Source:** Green, *The Gospel of Luke* (NICNT, 1997)  
**Section:** 5.5 The Unsettling Presence of the Kingdom through Kingdom Economics / Faithful Service (13:10–17:10); 5.6 Responding to the Kingdom (17:11–19:27)  
**Target slugs:** [[luke]], [[joel-green]], [[jesus]], [[jubilee]], [[theophilus]]

## Claims

### C1 — Section method: disciples formed indirectly; Pharisees as primary interlocutors
**Locus:** 8341–8347 (slice ll. 1–7)  
**Quote:** "The disciples, after all, appear explicitly only rarely in this section (16:1; 17:1, 5), and Jesus’ primary interaction is with Pharisees… programmatic questions… ‘Lord, will only a few be saved?’ (13:23); ‘Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God!’ (14:15)… what qualifies a person for fellowship in the community of God’s people… much of Jesus’ instruction… is set within or centers around occasions for table fellowship…"  
**Claim (Green):** In 13:10–17:10, Green reads Luke as forming disciples largely through conflict with Pharisees; boundary-making and community definition dominate; meals are the natural setting for those questions.

### C2 — Door of discipleship remains open to Pharisees; open-ended parables
**Locus:** 8347–8349 (slice ll. 13–15)  
**Quote:** "Clearly, the door of discipleship remains open, even to Pharisees… parables in 15:3–32 and 16:19–31 are open-ended; we do not know whether the elder brother… will join in the celebration… nor whether the five brothers… will actually hear Moses and the prophets… formation of disciples happens in front of the text too…"  
**Claim (Green):** Pharisees are not closed as a group; some warn Jesus (13:31); Jesus continues table instruction with them (chs. 14–16); Luke’s audience is also being formed. Fidelity is no basis for elevated status (17:7–10).

### C3 — Bent-over woman (13:10–17) programmatic for 13:10–17:10; Nazareth “release” fulfilled
**Locus:** 8351–8365 (slice ll. 19–33)  
**Quote:** "the conjunction, ‘therefore,’ in v 18… legitimate Jesus’ action in the synagogue as kingdom activity… nothing other than ‘… a marked fulfillment of the programme of the ministry as announced in the synagogue at Nazareth (4:18).’… 13:10–21 is programmatic for the narrative section that encompasses 13:10–17:10… Jesus’ encounter with this woman and his ensuing interpretation of her liberation as… presence of the kingdom, on this day, the Sabbath."  
**Claim (Green):** Sabbath synagogue reentry (first since 9:51) recalls Galilean synagogue teaching; healing as “release” fulfills 4:18–19 / Jubilee mission; focus is liberation of the woman, not merely legal controversy. Secondary: Green cites others on Nazareth fulfillment; biomedical spondylitis suggestions are bracketed—Luke attributes satanic bondage.

### C4 — “Daughter of Abraham”: low-status woman restored; honor-shame undercut
**Locus:** 8365–8397 (slice ll. 33–65)  
**Quote:** "this woman is painted in lowly dress indeed, rendering all the more significant Jesus’ recognition of her as ‘daughter of Abraham.’ This portends the extremely negative valuation Jesus will place on concerns rooted in the honor-shame system… ‘bent over’… metaphor for her ignominious social position… She is… one of those persons denoted by others as having no place among the people of God… yet raised up by God as children of Abraham…"  
**Claim (Green):** Abrahamic identity is gift of merciful restoration, not heroic credentials; healing liberates from satanic bondage and restores community membership; Jesus is “Lord,” divinely sanctioned hermeneut against the synagogue ruler’s self-evident Sabbath “ought.”

### C5 — Mustard seed and yeast legitimate lowly kingdom activity
**Locus:** 8401–8407 (slice ll. 69–75)  
**Quote:** "Jesus does not scour palatial grounds… he draws on first-century Palestinian village life… God’s kingdom is established through means other than the coercive power… satanic domination is being repealed and the kingdom of God is made present even in such seemingly inconsequential acts as the restoration of an ill woman who lived on the margins of society."  
**Claim (Green):** “Therefore” (13:18) ties kingdom parables to the healing; mustard “tree” + nesting birds (possible OT empire/bounty allusions) and leaven in “three measures” (food for ~150) image extravagant, invasive, non-elite dominion.

### C6 — “Will only a few be saved?” programmatic for inclusion/exclusion (13:22–30)
**Locus:** 8409–8417 (slice ll. 77–85)  
**Quote:** "a programmatic question is raised, ‘Are only a few people being saved?’ This is programmatic… for much of this larger section that runs from 13:10 to 17:10… group definition… Jesus’ response signals a profound departure… recalls the vision of Isaiah… Heredity, ancestral lineage as a Jew, does not figure into his reply… his image of the kingdom banquet is marked by its explicit embrace of the Gentile world."  
**Claim (Green):** Against narrowing Second Temple remnant trajectories (targum on Isa 25; 1 Enoch 62; Qumran excluding blemished Jews), Luke mirrors Isa 25:6–9’s universal banquet; present-tense “being saved” ties end-time vision to present reorientation around Jesus’ mission.

### C7 — Narrow door: ascription fails; performance (repentance, hearing and doing) counts
**Locus:** 8421–8439 (slice ll. 89–113)  
**Quote:** "Those seeking entrance do so apparently on the sole basis of their ascribed status… claim Abraham as their father… Failing this… claim association with Jesus… table fellowship as the occasion for receptivity… signified by repentance… authentic hearing… entails hearing and doing… Characterized as ‘doers of evil,’ these people… ties to Abraham and their previous association with Jesus count for nothing… status among those being saved is not inherited."  
**Claim (Green):** Owner-of-house figure maps onto Jesus’ future judgment role (Ps 6:8 intertext; Wisdom 2, 4–5 pattern); second-person “you” draws questioner, crowd, and Luke’s readers into the warning; first/last language overturns honor grounded in ancestry and purity performance.

### C8 — Entwined fates of Jesus and Jerusalem (13:31–35): divine purpose, judgment, conditional hope
**Locus:** 8449–8473 (slice ll. 117–145)  
**Quote:** "Jerusalem comes into the limelight… as the city that kills the prophets… motif of judgment is more prominent… Herod wants to kill Jesus; Jesus has wanted to restore and shelter… Jerusalemites have not wanted… ‘house’ will be abandoned… household of Jerusalem… centerpoint of practices and institutions… opposed to the will of God… If Israel will repent… and receive ‘the one who comes in the name of the Lord’… then Israel will recognize… salvation."  
**Claim (Green):** Some Pharisees warn Jesus without malevolent motive (parallel Acts 21:12–14); Herod as “fox” = destructive varmint impotent against divine necessity; Jerusalem as culture-center cipher for Israel; Ps 118:26 fulfilled by disciples at entry, not Jerusalem—foreshadowing rejection; judgment = God vacating the household. Secondary: Green rejects reading all Pharisees here as hostile distractors.

### C9 — Kingdom and banquet unit (14:1–24): symposium subverted; status transposition as salvation
**Locus:** 8475–8491 (slice ll. 147–159)  
**Quote:** "meals functioned to establish ‘in-group’ boundaries… Luke has drawn on the Greco-Roman tradition of the symposium… to show how Jesus’ message and practices departed… exclusionary and motivated by concerns for one’s honor… exaltation of the humble… inclusion of the excluded… Lukan theme of salvation, embodied… as ‘good news to the poor,’ and understood concretely in this scene as status transposition."  
**Claim (Green):** Host is leading Pharisee (elite invitees; watching Jesus closely); Jesus’ table rules grow from Spirit, merciful God, and present kingdom—not from Mediterranean honor/reciprocity. Green vs secondary: rejects purely elite-symposia description without conflict.

### C10 — Dropsy healing (14:1–6): Sabbath Jubilee; metaphorical diagnosis of greedy elite
**Locus:** 8493–8521 (slice ll. 161–189)  
**Quote:** "Jesus, in declaring the onset of the eschatological Jubilee (see above on 4:18–19), has made this day, even the Sabbath day… the day of divine benefaction for the needy… metaphorical use of ‘dropsy’ as a label for money-lovers… persons who share the very condition for which the Pharisees are indicted… Just as in front of Jesus stood a man who had dropsy, so, around the table, sat persons whose disorder was no less self-detrimental."  
**Claim (Green):** Parallel to 13:10–17 (release language; animal analogy; silence of opponents); healing + liberation coalesce; dropsical man as living parable of insatiable greed. Secondary: biomedical edema notes are Green’s framing, not Luke’s interest.

### C11 — Meal etiquette reversed (14:7–14): honor given not taken; invite those who cannot repay
**Locus:** 8525–8557 (slice ll. 193–259)  
**Quote:** "he is toppling the familiar world of the ancient Mediterranean… ‘all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.’… invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind… because they cannot repay you… ‘generalized reciprocity’… without expectation of return… ‘the righteous’ are those whose worldview is transformed… selfless generosity and redistribution on behalf of those… at the margins…"  
**Claim (Green):** V. 11 moves from strategic honor-management to divine valuation of the humble (Mary’s Song; good news to the poor); invitation lists deconstruct insider/outsider and patronage; resurrection of the righteous (first Lukan mention) linked to transformed table practice.

### C12 — Great banquet (14:15–24): elite host as transformed exemplar, not God as afterthought inviter of the poor
**Locus:** 8561–8607 (slice ll. 263–307)  
**Quote:** "Foremost is its unflattering portrait of God… as though God’s initial invitation list would have excluded ‘the poor’… But such a portrait is fundamentally at odds with Luke’s theology… An alternative reading… the prestigious company… would be lured into the story through their identification with the man who ‘gave a great dinner’… Will Jesus’ audience include the poor among their table intimates…? … no one is too sullied… He has participated in the creation of a new social order…"  
**Claim (Green):** Against common salvation-history allegory (Jews refuse → Gentiles/marginalized fill seats), Green reads host as model of elite conversion to Jesus’ 14:12–14 ethic; excuses mark wealth/family preoccupations; “compel” reflects socio-religious barriers, not mere etiquette; v. 24 addresses Jesus’/Luke’s elite audience. Secondary: Green explicitly rejects the majority allegorical reading.

### C13 — Cost of discipleship (14:25–35): hate family = redirected loyalty; renounce all; salt useless if unsalty
**Locus:** 8609–8637 (slice ll. 309–337)  
**Quote:** "‘hate’ is not primarily an affective quality but a disavowal of primary allegiance to one’s kin… reconstruction of one’s identity… within the new community oriented toward God’s purpose… none of you can become my disciple if you do not bid farewell to all you have… distinctive property of disciples is the abandonment… of all competing securities… those who attempt to journey with Jesus without a thoroughgoing commitment… are not worthy of the designation of ‘disciple.’"  
**Claim (Green):** Crowds as disciple pool (cf. 13:26–27 warning); tower/king parables insist existing resources (kin networks) are insufficient; salt saying (8:8 echo) urges authentic hearing against cares/riches/pleasures.

### C14 — Luke 15 unity: defense of table with sinners + open invitation to Pharisees
**Locus:** 8639–8647 (slice ll. 339–347)  
**Quote:** "three parables… cumulative response to the indictment… ‘This fellow welcomes sinners and eats with them.’… (1) Jesus’ defense of his ministry as an outworking of God’s own purpose and (2) Jesus’ implicit and open-ended invitation… to join him in reflecting… God’s own attitude toward sinners… As the chapter closes, the query remains open whether the Pharisees and legal experts will… join the celebration at the table…"  
**Claim (Green):** Ch. 15 is discrete (audience/setting through 16:1) yet organically tied to chs. 14 and 16 hospitality themes; heavenly joy vs. Pharisaic grumbling is the contrast.

### C15 — Setting 15:1–2: toll collectors/sinners hear; scribes/Pharisees grumble; Jesus generates new kin
**Locus:** 8649–8665 (slice ll. 349–363)  
**Quote:** "concrete illustration of… toll collectors… who ‘justified God,’ and the Pharisees and legal experts as those who ‘rejected God’s purpose’… Jesus… behaves toward these outsiders… as though they were his own kin… new group… outsiders whose status has been reversed… and ratified by their repentance… identifies with Jesus’ opponents any persons among Luke’s readers whose practices of table fellowship are similarly closed."  
**Claim (Green):** Parallel 5:29–32 (wilderness-generation grumbling echo); Jesus both receives and extends hospitality to sinners; Theophilus/Luke’s discourse situation still contested over table boundaries.

### C16 — Lost sheep and coin: theological portraits of God’s joy over repentant sinners
**Locus:** 8669–8697 (slice ll. 369–397)  
**Quote:** "these parables are fundamentally about God… divine response to the recovery of the lost… metaphorical representation of God first as a relatively wealthy shepherd, then as an impoverished widow… contrast between the complaints and grumbling… and the joy and festivity characteristic of God… emphasis… on the consequence of recovery, the necessity of celebration… not… how one is restored."  
**Claim (Green):** Parallel structure + escalation (1/100 → 1/10 → 1/2 sons); Ezek 34 echo indicts leaders and commends Jesus as Yahweh-like seeker; repentance assumed, celebration mandated; inviting friends implies festive meal tied to 15:1–2 charge.

### C17 — Prodigal: center is contrasting responses to recovery, not primarily the father alone
**Locus:** 8701–8715 (slice ll. 401–417)  
**Quote:** "center stage belongs to the younger son—and especially to the contrasting patterns of response occasioned by his recovery… father elevates such celebration to the level of divine necessity… Against… Roman… paterfamilias… authoritarianism… the picture Luke paints is remarkable for its counteremphasis on care and compassion."  
**Claim (Green):** Green modifies traditional “father with two sons” title-focus: dual segments (father’s compassion vs. elder’s anger); kinship redefined (son vs. hireling/slave; “this son of yours” vs. “this brother of yours”); open ending = open invitation to Pharisees.

### C18 — Younger son: death/loss to life/found; father’s initiative before full confession
**Locus:** 8717–8735 (slice ll. 419–435)  
**Quote:** "his request clearly signifies his rejection of his family… ‘distant country’… non-Jewish world… pigs… ‘he came to himself’… shades of repentance… it is the younger son’s return, and not his confession, that makes reconciliation possible… confession… cut short… father has already launched a full restoration… compassion… robe, ring, and sandals… fatted calf… ‘this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found!’"  
**Claim (Green):** Estate divided “between them” (elder already has his share); downward mobility toward “expendables”; banquet = lavish recovery celebration paralleling sheep/coin; “heaven” language links to 15:7.

### C19 — Elder son: angry refusal of table = self-exclusion; invitation to join divine necessity of joy
**Locus:** 8737–8747 (slice ll. 437–447)  
**Quote:** "refusal to enter… refusal to share in the meal, a symbolic act of gargantuan proportions… does not name him as ‘Father’… younger son is only ‘this son of yours’… ironically… comports himself now not as a son but as a slave… father… advances a condition—namely, that the elder acknowledge the divine necessity of celebrating… Will they… join repentant sinners at the table?… The parable is open-ended, and so is the invitation."  
**Claim (Green):** Maps elder → scribes/Pharisees; younger → repentant toll collectors/sinners; Jesus’ table = father’s grace; refusal to embrace God’s “gracious calculus” risks self-exclusion from the family of God.

### C20 — Ch. 16 kingdom economics: wealth for hospitality to the poor who cannot reciprocate
**Locus:** 8749–8757 (slice ll. 449–457)  
**Quote:** "Faithfulness to God is demonstrated in the extension of hospitality to the poor. Such hospitality occasions the redistribution of wealth to those incapable of reciprocation, underscores the importance of the creation of friendship across social boundaries, and secures an eternal home… Pharisees… dramatic counterexample…"  
**Claim (Green):** Audience shift to disciples is artificial (Pharisees eavesdrop 16:14); organic link to 14–15 table themes; linguistic parallels between 15:11–32 and 16:1–8; Lazarus//younger son status-reversal parallel.

### C21 — Dishonest manager (16:1–9): shrewdness of this age → children of light use mammon to make friends
**Locus:** 8759–8787 (slice ll. 459–487)  
**Quote:** "make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth so that when it is gone, they may welcome you into the eternal homes… master does not commend his manager for his dishonesty, but for his prudence… ‘Children of this age’… why do ‘children of light’ not understand the ways of the kingdom… Jesus provides no basis… for… reciprocation… alms to the poor… genuine social solidarity between rich and poor, who act toward each other as ‘equal friends.’"  
**Claim (Green):** Not allegory of God/Jesus; everyday patronage script; debt reduction creates binding benefaction; mammon is “dishonest” as belonging to this aeon and destined to vanish; dualism is eschatological, not Platonic cosmological.

### C22 — Faithful in little (16:10–13): cannot serve God and Wealth; stewardship of Yahweh’s property
**Locus:** 8789–8805 (slice ll. 489–505)  
**Quote:** "Faithfulness… evidenced in the cancellation of debts and in almsgiving… Wealth is either used faithfully… or… takes on a personified, cosmological status… You cannot serve God and Wealth… OT understanding of Yahweh as the true owner… property and land are to be used for the good of all… forging relationships with the poor that signal… eschatological reversal."  
**Claim (Green):** “True riches” = heavenly/unfailing treasure (12:33); opposition of masters is practical/worldview, not eternal dualism of equal powers; Josephus/Essene community-of-goods noted as partial parallel (secondary).

### C23 — Pharisees as “lovers of money” (16:14–18): law and wealth as one theme; abomination
**Locus:** 8807–8837 (slice ll. 507–537)  
**Quote:** "Luke has departed from what we know of the historical Pharisees, providing his own polemical evaluation… ‘lovers of money’… wealth had value proportional to… status honor… neglect the poor for the sake of their own community status… what is prized by human beings is an abomination in the sight of God… good news of the kingdom… ‘everyone is urged to enter it’… enduring validity of the law… divorce… surprisingly rigorous interpretation… idolatry, wealth, and divorce… collocated as manifestations of pseudo-righteousness."  
**Claim (Green):** Irony: Pharisees charge Jesus with relaxing law while they transgress Scripture by neglecting the poor; new era from John expands grace without nullifying law; Damascus Rule “three nets” intertext (secondary support). Wordplay: friends of money vs. make friends with mammon (16:9).

### C24 — Rich man and Lazarus (16:19–31): gate becomes fixed chasm; Moses and prophets suffice
**Locus:** 8839–8885 (slice ll. 539–585)  
**Quote:** "social distance… symbolized first by the gate, then by… ‘great chasm’… poor man’s only claim to status is that he is named… wealthy man… no name… eschatological reversal… Lazarus… received no comfort, is now comforted… gate that could have been traversed but was not… has now become fixed… ‘They have Moses and the prophets’… If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets, neither will they be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.’… in neglecting the poor, they have disregarded the will of God so clearly expressed in the Scriptures."  
**Claim (Green):** Directed at money-loving Pharisees; rich man still treats Lazarus as errand-boy; claims “Father Abraham” without repentant life (3:8); eleos/eleēmosynē wordplay; brothers’ circle of compassion still only kin (14:12–14); gate echoes Amos 5 justice-in-the-gate; no apocalyptic return of the dead allowed.

### C25 — Faithful service (17:1–10): close of “who participates?”; do not be like Pharisees
**Locus:** 8887–8917 (slice ll. 587–617)  
**Quote:** "vv 1–10 form the end of the lengthy section—concerned with the question, Who will participate in the kingdom?—that began in 13:10… ‘Do not be like the Pharisees’… millstone… than for you to cause one of these little ones to stumble… little ones… Lazarus… lost son… poor, crippled, blind, and lame… forgiveness ‘seven times’… without limit… ‘We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done!’… obedience [not] a means to gain honor…"  
**Claim (Green):** Fluid borders disciples/Pharisees still; faith as disposition producing faithfulness; master-slave parable rejects reward-seeking (echo elder brother’s quest for recognition); mustard-seed faith sufficient for extraordinary restorative practices.

### C26 — 17:11–19:27 as thematic summary: journey quickens; faith/faithfulness and eschatological division
**Locus:** 8919–8937 (slice ll. 619–637)  
**Quote:** "critical role of ‘thematic summary’ and invitation to response… destination is Jerusalem… he denies that his advent signals the eschatological arrival of the kingdom… Son of Man ‘must endure much suffering’… interlude… ‘days of the Son of Man’… ‘find faith on earth’… list of candidates… a leper, Samaritan, foreigner… widow… toll collector… infants… Zacchaeus… Will the Son of Man find faithfulness?"  
**Claim (Green):** Disciples still misunderstand suffering, honor, and mission; exemplary responders are the marginalized; proper identification of Jesus correlates with faith.

### C27 — Ten lepers (17:11–19): Samaritan “foreigner” returns; faith saves beyond cleansing
**Locus:** 8939–8987 (slice ll. 639–687)  
**Quote:** "Only in v 16b does Luke drop the bombshell—‘and he was a Samaritan’… challenge notions of the privileged position of the Jewish people… Naaman… intertextuality… outsiders may receive… salvation… He does not travel to a temple, but returns to Jesus… Jesus in the role of the temple… ‘your faith has saved you’… something more than healing… insight into Jesus’ role in the inbreaking kingdom… not because of his status as a Jew… ancestry and… purity."  
**Claim (Green):** Border Galilee/Samaria ambiguity; ten cleansed, one perceives/praises/thanks; christological height—worship at Jesus’ feet mediates Jew/Samaritan temple divide; “foreigner” temple-inscription irony (secondary). Jubilee/good-news-to-poor trajectory continues.

### C28 — Kingdom among you (17:20–21): Pharisees wrong on exclusive futurity and observation
**Locus:** 8993–9013 (slice ll. 693–713)  
**Quote:** "The question posed by the Pharisees is wrongheaded on two counts… exclusively a future entity… through scientific observation… the kingdom of God is among you… already active… closely related to the person and activity of Jesus… Pharisees do not recognize… God’s new world order."  
**Claim (Green):** Contrast with discerning Samaritan leper; kingdom not localizable to place/nation (cf. Acts 1:6–8); disciples also need this correction (17:22–37).

### C29 — Son of Man coming (17:22–37): unmistakable day; suffering first; lose life to keep it
**Locus:** 9015–9061 (slice ll. 715–761)  
**Quote:** "that ‘day’ as unmistakable, worldwide, sudden, inescapable… ‘first he must endure much suffering and be rejected by this generation’… days of Noah/Lot… everyday life… suddenly interrupted… Remember Lot’s wife… Those who try to make their life secure will lose it… Where the corpse is, there the vultures will gather."  
**Claim (Green):** A-B-C-B′-A′ structure centers readiness; day/days distinguish present career (incl. church) and eschaton; theologia crucis as narrative of faithful discipleship; division finalizes Simeon’s prophecy (2:34–35); “where?” is moot.

### C30 — Persistent widow (18:1–8): pray always; God grants justice; will Son of Man find *the* faith?
**Locus:** 9063–9097 (slice ll. 763–797)  
**Quote:** "need to pray always and not to lose heart… Will he delay long… he will quickly grant justice… when the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?… ‘the faith’—that is, that manner of faith demonstrated by the widow… ‘prayer’… metonym for confidence… openness to the benefaction of God… active quest for justice… astonishing persistence."  
**Claim (Green):** Lesser-to-greater from unjust judge to God; Sir 35 echo without vengeance motif (secondary); widow models elect who cry day and night; reorients eschatology from When?/Where? to How will people respond?

### C31 — Pharisee and toll collector (18:9–14): self-possessed righteousness vs. mercy-seeking humility
**Locus:** 9105–9181 (slice ll. 805–881)  
**Quote:** "some who relied on themselves because they were righteous and regarded others with contempt… Pharisee’s prayer… enumerates… his own [acts]… toll collector… ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’… this man went down to his home justified rather than the other; for all who exalt themselves will be humbled…"  
**Claim (Green):** Audience not only Pharisees—disciples also susceptible (9:46–50; 12:1); temple as culture-center of segregation; Pharisee’s thanksgiving form empty of God’s acts; exalt/humble proverb reprises 14:11; toll collector included among God’s people as other “sinners” in Luke.

### C32 — Children and kingdom (18:15–17): receive kingdom as one receives a little child
**Locus:** 9183–9197 (slice ll. 883–897)  
**Quote:** "disciples… sternly ordered them not to… ‘the kingdom of God consists of such as these’… ‘Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will never enter it.’… ellipsis: ‘as one receives a little child’… extend respectful service to that social group most often overlooked… disciples find themselves contesting the divine purpose…"  
**Claim (Green):** Children as low-status “not adults,” not romantic innocence; disciples’ obstruction parallels later barriers (blind man, Zacchaeus); hospitality ethic subverts honor canons.

### C33 — Rich ruler (18:18–30): wealth blocks kingdom entry; disciples partially rehabilitated
**Locus:** 9199–9251 (slice ll. 899–951)  
**Quote:** "How hard it is for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!… camel… eye of a needle… ‘What is impossible for mortals is possible for God.’… ‘Sell all that you own and distribute the money to the poor’… not… poverty as an ascetic ideal… disposition… for the sake of the poor… Peter… ‘we have left what is ours and followed you’… get back very much more in this age, and in the age to come eternal life."  
**Claim (Green):** Juxtaposed with children as status-transposition illustration of 18:14; “good teacher” honor-game rejected; Decalogue community-relations baseline expanded to almsgiving without return; common theology equating wealth with blessing grips ruler and hearers; disciples distinguished from ruler yet still need resocialization.

### C34 — Third passion prediction (18:31–34): prophets fulfilled; disciples still uncomprehending
**Locus:** 9253–9267 (slice ll. 953–967)  
**Quote:** "everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished… handed over to the Gentiles… mocked and insulted and spat upon… kill him, and on the third day he will rise again.’ But they understood nothing… what he said was hidden from them…"  
**Claim (Green):** Divine necessity + Jerusalem destiny; Gentile culpability added to earlier Jewish-leadership prediction (9:22); humiliation as status-reversal center of salvation; disciples’ blindness matches failure with children and honor values.

### C35 — Blind man at Jericho (18:35–43): Son of David mercy; faith saves; follows glorifying God
**Locus:** 9269–9299 (slice ll. 969–999)  
**Quote:** "‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!’… ‘those in front’… ordered him to be quiet… ‘Lord, let me see again.’… ‘your faith has saved you.’… followed him, glorifying God… people who fail to comprehend that the divine plan is oriented to salvation as status reversal—will hardly anticipate the gift of salvation… to such social refuse as a blind beggar."  
**Claim (Green):** First public “Son of David” declaration; “those in front” as status-first obstruction (discipleship irony); salvation = sight + social potential + entry into Jesus’ kin/discipleship; exemplifies 18:9–19:27 fitness theme.

### C36 — Zacchaeus (19:1–10): today salvation; son of Abraham by practice; Son of Man seeks the lost
**Locus:** 9301–9355 (slice ll. 1001–1055)  
**Quote:** "‘I must stay at your house today.’… ‘Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek out and to save the lost.’… Luke dismisses the usual, stereotypical categories… ruler, toll collector, wealthy, and sinner… determination of one’s inclusion… Do you conduct yourself as a child of Abraham?"  
**Claim (Green):** Tight foil to rich ruler (both rulers/wealthy; opposite outcomes); crowd as barrier (not merely height); joyous hospitality = receptivity; “I give… I pay back” as present progressive customary practice of justice/almsgiving, not conversion resolve mid-scene—vindication, not first-time spiritual conversion (Green’s distinctive reading against common “futuristic present” conversion reading). Salvation = Jesus’ presence restoring household to God’s people; Ezek 34 intertext (seek the lost).

### C37 — Zacchaeus possessions: half to poor + fourfold restitution as kingdom economics, not half-discipleship
**Locus:** 9337–9345 (slice ll. 1037–1045)  
**Quote:** "What are we to make of Zacchaeus’s failure to disinvest himself completely…? … almsgiving… including in one’s circle of kin those who are unable to reciprocate… ‘make friends’ via giving without expectation of return… Unlike the rich ruler, Zacchaeus does not employ his wealth so as to procure honor and friends; rather… puts his possessions in the service of the needy and of justice."  
**Claim (Green):** Resolves 18:22 // 19:8 tension by function of wealth (status-seeking vs. solidarity), not by a single absolute percentage rule.

### C38 — Pounds/minas (19:11–27): kingdom not immediate at Jerusalem; faithfulness while the king is away
**Locus:** 9357–9397 (slice ll. 1057–1097)  
**Quote:** "because he was near Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately… certainty of the ‘appearance’ of the kingdom, but… shifts the focus from the question of when to the issue of faithfulness in anticipation… Jesus was first to meet death, not the consummation of the kingdom, in Jerusalem… trustworthy in a very small thing… enemies… who did not want me to be king… slaughter them…"  
**Claim (Green):** Ties to Zacchaeus “today” raising timetable questions; Archelaus parallel supplies realism (secondary Josephus); resists simple allegory equating nobleman=Jesus (harsh exploiter traits) or citizens=“the Jews” (anti-Semitism charge untenable); ironic christological edge—kingdom that includes Zacchaeus seems harsh to status-seekers; judgment on refusal of the rule as defined by Jesus’ mission to the marginalized.

### C39 — Status reversal as through-line of late travel narrative
**Locus:** multiple (esp. 8347; 8489–8491; 8557; 8839–8857; 9105–9197; 9309–9311)  
**Quote:** "those who are last will be first… all who exalt themselves will be humbled… status transposition… eschatological reversal… salvation as status reversal…"  
**Claim (Green):** From Magnificat through 13:30; 14:11; 16:19–31; 18:14; children; blind man; Zacchaeus, Green treats status reversal as Lukan soteriology’s concrete social form—good news to the poor enacted in table, wealth, and community boundaries.

### C40 — Banquet/table as primary kingdom image for inclusion-exclusion
**Locus:** multiple (esp. 8345–8347; 8409–8439; 8475–8607; 8639–8747; 8807–8885)  
**Quote:** "Questions of boundary-making and community definition are very much at home at meals… eat in the kingdom of God… Blessed is anyone who will eat bread in the kingdom of God… Rejoice with me… fatted calf… welcome me into their homes… eternal homes…"  
**Claim (Green):** Table fellowship is where Luke stages who belongs: eschatological banquet (Isa 25), Pharisee meals, Lost celebrations, mammon-made friends, rich man’s daily feasts vs. Lazarus. Inclusion is repentance + hospitality without reciprocity; exclusion is status-ascription, greed, and refusal of the recovered.

### C41 — Jerusalem foreshadowed: prophet-killing city, abandoned house, suffering before kingdom consummation
**Locus:** 8449–8473; 8919–8931; 9253–9267; 9357–9365 (slice ll. 117–145, 619–631, 953–967, 1057–1065)  
**Quote:** "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets… your house is abandoned… journey… destination is Jerusalem… must endure much suffering and be rejected… near Jerusalem… supposed that the kingdom… appear immediately… first to meet death, not the consummation of the kingdom, in Jerusalem."  
**Claim (Green):** 13:31–35 and later passion/journey notices bind Jesus’ fate to Jerusalem’s judgment and delayed kingdom consummation; disciples’ misunderstanding of this timetable is a major late-travel problem.

### C42 — Jubilee / good news to the poor as hermeneutical key for healings and economics

### C43 — Theophilus/readers: formation “in front of the text”; closed tables indicted
**Locus:** 8347–8349; 8663–8665; 8919–8937

**Claim (Green):** Commentary continually addresses [[theophilus]]/model readers as co-addressees of open-ended invitations (elder brother, five brothers, elite hosts, disciples) and warnings against Pharisaic honor/money habits.

### C44 — Hermeneutic of Scripture: Moses and prophets require kingdom-shaped reading, not nullification
**Locus:** 8825–8837; 8867–8885; 9253–9261  
**Quote:** "Jesus is not abrogating the law… Scriptures of Israel must be understood in light of the manifestation of God’s purpose within the ministry of Jesus… If they do not listen to Moses and the prophets… everything that is written about the Son of Man by the prophets will be accomplished."  
**Claim (Green):** Law’s ethical demand realized in care for the poor (neighbor-love, 10:25–37); resurrection/someone from the dead will not persuade those who ignore Scripture’s poor; passion fulfills prophetic witness as whole, not isolated proof-texts.

### C45 — Who will be saved? Summary synthesis of Green’s answer in this span
**Locus:** section-wide (13:23–30; 14:15–24; 15; 16:19–31; 18:9–30; 19:1–10)  
**Quote:** "life with God in the eschaton is directly related to identifying fully, personally, and in the present with the redemptive aim of God manifest in Jesus’ mission… Performance, understood as repentance, as hearing and doing the word… those who… embrace a new social order governed by the kingdom of God with its concern for the destitute and outcast."  
**Claim (Green):** Salvation is present communal reorientation (not mere heredity or past association with Jesus); marked by repentance, humility, unreciprocated hospitality/alms, renunciation of competing securities, and recognition of Jesus as divine agent; self-exalting, money-loving, obstructive “righteous” risk exclusion even while patriarchs, prophets, Gentiles, sinners, children, and “lost” sons of Abraham feast.
